description:
## Question

Elixir mode is normative (see "Should a kernel body also run as plain Elixir?"): every C/Elixir disagreement is a bug unless it is a listed divergence. How is agreement checked: which input generators (edge values such as i64 overflow boundaries, empty and length-1 arrays, out-of-bounds indices, division by zero, extreme floats), which tests run in both modes (catalog kernels, the subset's own tests, every docs/language.md example), how errors are compared (same exception type and message?), and what the check costs in CI time.

comments.text: Per 'What is the one rule a kernel author keeps in their head?' (defk-dtw.7): the generators must deliberately cover out-of-range array writes, i64 overflow boundaries, inf/NaN-producing operations and aliasing patterns; these tests replace a manual audit of differences.

Per 'Which open runtime issues are safety gaps?' (defk-dtw.12): the differential tests also run once with kernels built under AddressSanitizer/UBSan, and the generators include huge and negative sizes (alloc lengths near 2^61/2^63; see bug defk-gtv).

Resolution:
- Elixir mode applies the subset's limits (i64 range after every integer op, writes that don't fit raise, same exception modules as the kernel), so agreement is exact. A missing limit shows up as a disagreement.
- Agreement: values === (bit-exact floats, -0.0 /= 0.0); raises match on module plus a normalised reason, not message text.
- Floats: kernels build with -ffp-contract=off, never fast-math; reordering float ops is a divergence. C supplies speed through everything that keeps Elixir's answer (bounds-check removal, integer vectorisation, if-conversion, -O3, restrict) and protection through hardening flags (adopted if under 2%).
- Inputs: StreamData (test-only). Type-derived, edge-biased generators from each signature, an optional per-kernel workload generator, and hostile-argument generators (wrong types, bad lengths, sub/unaligned/refc/heap binaries) where only a raise is allowed. Aliasing and inf/NaN go in hand-written subset tests.
- Scope: catalog kernels (assert_agrees), every subset test (Defk.Case runs each test body in both modes), and docs/language.md examples (doctest-style extractor; rejected examples are checked for their error code).
- Known divergences go in a Defk.Divergences registry that generates the divergence page; done requires it to be empty.
- Cost: default mix test at about 100 runs per property, suite under about 60s. A manual deep run (about 10k runs in a :peer node, so a VM crash becomes a shrunk failure) plus an ASan/UBSan run, recorded in the verdict's method section. No CI.
- Never taking down the BEAM is part of the runtime contract's definition (CONTEXT.md) and a done condition: for any arguments a kernel returns or raises, never starves or crashes the VM; otherwise a port is the better choice.
Build: defk-v5d (Build Elixir mode) -> defk-63k (Differential agreement checks), which blocks the six catalog workloads; defk-jlk (-ffp-contract=off) blocks defk-63k; defk-rhb (docs/language.md examples); defk-j5n (hardening flags).

title: How are kernels checked against Elixir mode?
